title: Towards Robust and Generalized Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Noisy Label Learning
peft_method: Adapter; BitFit; prompt tuning; LoRA with CleaR
extra_training_stages: 3-10 epoch warm-up followed by epoch-wise routing
core_mechanism: fits a two-component GMM to cached previous-epoch losses; samples an independent Bernoulli routing decision at every transformer layer; likely-noisy examples bypass PEFT modules; consistency regularization uses cached ensemble predictions
main_claim: clean-probability routing protects limited PEFT capacity from noisy interference while mitigating PEFT underfitting on clean examples
mechanism_evidence: 10-seed SST-5 experiments; TREC and 20NewsGroups appendix; symmetric asymmetric and instance-dependent synthetic label noise; component and routing ablations
efficiency_reported: 20 fine-tuning epochs; four RTX 3090 GPUs; five-forward ensemble for consistency but predictions are reused for GMM; no end-to-end wall-clock or VRAM comparison
strongest_result: CleaR variants consistently improve peak and late-epoch average accuracy over their underlying PEFT methods; gains are largest in high-noise settings
reported_limitations: encoder-only evaluation; all evaluated noise is synthetic; warm-up epoch gamma and learning rate are selected from sweeps; wall-clock overhead is asserted negligible but not measured
direct_prior_risk: critical: direct prior for loss-based online clean routing in PEFT
audit_notes: Deep-read 2026-07-31. No clean reference or known noise rate is required by the mechanism. The paper's hyperparameter selection protocol is not sufficiently separated from a clean-development assumption to support a no-clean-validation claim.

title: Fine-tuning Pre-trained Models for Robustness under Noisy Labels
backbone_family: ViT-B/16; ConvNeXt-T; MAE-ViT-B; MSN-ViT-B; CLIP-ViT-B; ResNet-50
core_mechanism: pre-extracts frozen features; trains a linear classifier with GCE for 20 epochs; then fits per-class GMMs to sample losses each epoch, selects a class-balanced subset above threshold 0.6, and full-fine-tunes for four epochs
main_claim: linear probing buffers pretrained features against severe unknown label noise; repeated cleansing makes later full fine-tuning safe and cheap
mechanism_evidence: three-trial CIFAR-100 experiments with symmetric asymmetric and instance-dependent noise; Clothing1M and WebVision; six pretrained architectures; component and hyperparameter analyses
efficiency_reported: TURN uses 20 LP plus four FFT epochs and reports 0.12 times UNICON training time while improving accuracy by 2.69 points in the CIFAR-100 90-percent symmetric setting; features are cached during LP
strongest_result: on ViT-B/16 CIFAR-100 with 90-percent symmetric noise TURN reports 84.35 percent versus 80.72 DivideMix and 80.23 UNICON
reported_limitations: per-class uniform selection can discard valid data under natural class imbalance; GMM threshold and LP/FFT durations require tuning; Ray search cost is excluded; defect scope is label noise only
direct_prior_risk: critical: direct prior for cheap two-stage pretrained-model filtering without known noise rate
audit_notes: Deep-read 2026-07-31. The paper has no dedicated limitations section. Baseline comparisons move expensive DivideMix and UNICON to linear probing because of compute limits, so cross-method resource comparisons need qualification.

title: Weed Out, Then Harvest: Dual Low-Rank Adaptation is an Effective Noisy Label Detector for Noise-Robust Learning
clean_reference_required: yes: clean development set for hyperparameter selection; GPT-4o supplies pseudo-positive labels and relabeling
extra_models: dual LoRA detector; GPT-4o; separate downstream classifier
core_mechanism: constrains clean-LoRA and noisy-LoRA update magnitudes in opposite temporal directions; compares their per-sample losses as a learned detector; constructs detector positives with GPT-4o agreement and negatives with random label flips; then GPT-4o relabels detected noisy samples before classifier training
main_claim: parameter-level separation breaks the feedback loop between small-loss selection and classifier fitting and turns dual LoRA into a high-precision noisy-label detector
mechanism_evidence: five synthetic text benchmarks with 20 and 40 percent symmetric asymmetric and instance-dependent noise; three real-noise text datasets; detector classifier and loss ablations
efficiency_reported: eight detector epochs including two warm-up epochs plus six classifier epochs; RTX 3090 and A100; on Llama-3.1-8B the method uses 27.3M trainable parameters and 13.6GB versus 13.7M and 10.4GB for single LoRA; GPT-4o calls and clean-dev selection cost are not included
strongest_result: on TREC the method reports up to 10 accuracy points over single LoRA and substantially higher detection precision and recall than small-loss and direct GPT-4o detection
reported_limitations: Findings rather than ACL main; text classification only; no 70B evaluation; external GPT-4o cost and reproducibility are material; clean-development hyperparameter selection and two-stage training weaken the low-resource claim
direct_prior_risk: critical: direct prior for dual-adapter temporal separation and noise detection
audit_notes: Deep-read 2026-07-31. Must not describe Delora as self-contained or no-clean-reference: GPT-4o is used twice and hyperparameters are selected on a clean development set.

title: Why LoRA Resists Label Noise: A Theoretical Framework for Noise-Robust Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning
peft_method: RACT with rank-4 and rank-16 LoRA
noise_assumed_known: threshold may use estimated noise rate
clean_reference_required: optional: held-out known-label validation is recommended for threshold calibration
core_mechanism: derives rank-dependent memorization capacity, a qualitative noise-rank tradeoff, and temporal separation; RACT trains low- and high-rank adapters, flags large negative loss discrepancies as noise, and optionally retrains the low-rank adapter on retained data
main_claim: LoRA's rank constraint limits arbitrary-label memorization and rank discrepancy can expose mislabeled samples
mechanism_evidence: theorems plus AG News IMDB MNIST and CIFAR-10 experiments; three main NLP seeds but some IMDB and baseline results use two or one seed; symmetric label noise only
efficiency_reported: training two adapters doubles training time; NLP phase 1 is 10 epochs and optional retraining is five; experiments use a workstation with 36GB RAM but GPU is not disclosed
strongest_result: AG News at 30-percent noise reports 91.27 F1 and 91.47 accuracy for rank pair 4 and 16
reported_limitations: single-author preprint; medium-scale benchmarks; symmetric noise only; threshold tuning requires validation or noise-rate estimation; theory uses existential capacity bounds, squared loss, linearization, signal smoothness, and asymptotic arguments that are not tight deep-network guarantees
direct_prior_risk: critical: direct prior for rank scheduling rank discrepancy temporal separation and two-adapter PEFT detection
audit_notes: Deep-read 2026-07-31. The paper is not peer reviewed as of the audit date. Treat theorem-guided rank claims as a high-risk preprint prior, not established fact.

title: Compute-Constrained Data Selection
clean_reference_required: yes: target-task validation set assumed IID with test
core_mechanism: defines total cost as selector cost plus training cost and compares random BM25 embedding perplexity and gradient-based LESS under matched FLOP budgets; fits a saturating compute-performance model
main_claim: selectors must improve training in proportion to their own cost; expensive perplexity and gradient selectors are usually not compute-optimal
mechanism_evidence: more than 600 runs across three target tasks six selectors 7B-70B model sizes and varying token budgets
efficiency_reported: BM25 is treated as near-zero FLOPs; embedding costs 4.4e16; perplexity 1.53e18; LESS 8.27e18 including four-epoch warm-up on five percent plus a gradient pass; perplexity and gradient selection need roughly 5x and 10x training-to-selector model-size ratios
strongest_result: cheap BM25 or embedding selection dominates most compute-constrained Pareto fronts; LESS needs cost amortization across many tasks to break even
reported_limitations: only one fine-tuning epoch; fixed hyperparameters; IID validation-test and monotone/submodular utility assumptions; instruction-fine-tuning tasks rather than unknown defects; wall-clock and memory are not the primary budget metric
direct_prior_risk: critical: kills novelty of counting selector cost inside a fixed total budget
audit_notes: Deep-read 2026-07-31. This paper does not solve noisy-data identification, but it establishes the mandatory accounting protocol and cheap-selector baselines for our work.

title: Computational Budget Should Be Considered in Data Selection
clean_reference_required: yes: outer objective evaluates on a held-out validation set; CIFAR-10 reserves 5000 clean examples
extra_models: bilevel learner plus one-dimensional loss estimator or surrogate
core_mechanism: casts which examples or sources and how many samples to process as bilevel optimization under a sample-usage budget; uses probabilistic reparameterization, Hessian-free policy gradients, and a penalty relaxation; CADS-E selects examples and CADS-S learns source sampling ratios
main_claim: the compute budget changes the optimal mix of data quantity quality and distribution, including how much noisy-source data should be used
mechanism_evidence: MNIST; CIFAR-10 with five sources at 0 22.5 45 67.5 and 90 percent label noise; DomainNet; GPT-2 with Alpaca sources; 13 instruction datasets
efficiency_reported: all experiments use one A100 80GB; paper reports 3-20 times speedup over conventional bilevel implementations and a cost expression of (5/A+2gamma)C with reuse amortization; selection investment is explicitly assumed reusable
strongest_result: on CIFAR-10 at 225000 sample usages CADS-S reports 67.22 percent versus 65.08 best-source and 57.03 full-dataset; maximum reported gain across tasks is 14.42 points
reported_limitations: budget is measured mainly in sample-processing steps and may not match wall-clock or sparse-model cost; requires validation feedback; source-level results assume known group membership; selection cost is justified through reuse amortization; large-scale statistical testing is incomplete
direct_prior_risk: critical: directly covers compute-aware allocation across label-noise sources
audit_notes: Deep-read 2026-07-31. This is the strongest killer of the broad project framing. A surviving contribution must remove or challenge at least one of its clean-validation, grouped-source, reusable-coreset, or budget-metric assumptions while retaining competitive accuracy.

title: MATES: Model-Aware Data Selection for Efficient Pretraining with Data Influence Models
clean_reference_required: yes: a reference task and a same-distribution hold-out pool are required
core_mechanism: every 10000 steps locally probes one-step updates on hold-out examples against LAMBADA reference loss; fits BERT-base to oracle influence; scores the corpus and samples a 20-percent subset with Gumbel-Top-k
main_claim: a model-aware scorer can follow the learner's changing data preference more efficiently than static quality or influence rules
mechanism_evidence: C4 pretraining for 25B tokens; nine zero-shot tasks; reference-task update-frequency scorer-scale and sampling-ratio analyses
efficiency_reported: selection is 21.7 percent of total FLOPs for 410M and 11.5 percent for 1B; experiments use eight A6000 GPUs for two or four days; collecting 160000 oracle scores takes about 14 hours; influence-model inference dominates selector cost
strongest_result: average downstream accuracy improves 1.3 points at 410M and 1.1 points at 1B over random selection while shifting the compute-performance curve
reported_limitations: assumes pointwise independent influence and ignores interactions; depends on reference-task choice; moderate 410M-1B scale; auxiliary model and local probes are incompatible with a strict one-GPU budget without redesign
direct_prior_risk: critical: direct prior for time-varying learned sample utility
audit_notes: Deep-read 2026-07-31. MATES is not a noisy-label method and its compute regime is far outside ours, but any online learned-value scorer must explain why it is not a small-scale MATES analogue.

title: Handling Label Noise via Instance-Level Difficulty Modeling and Dynamic Optimization
peft_method: linear probing or full fine-tuning in stage one
core_mechanism: accumulates per-example wrong events across epochs; fits a class-wise two-component beta mixture to infer cleanliness and a U-shaped difficulty score; stage two dynamically blends supervised pseudo-label and two-view consistency losses
main_claim: wrong-event history remains stable after loss begins fitting noise and jointly exposes cleanliness and difficulty without manual noise-rate hyperparameters
mechanism_evidence: five-run CIFAR-10/100 Tiny-ImageNet CIFAR-100N Clothing1M and WebVision experiments; symmetric asymmetric instance-dependent and real noise; metric loss and component analyses
efficiency_reported: five stage-one plus ten stage-two epochs on one A100 80GB; ViT-B/16 takes 458 seconds and 14.8GB per epoch versus DivideMix 1596 seconds and 31.8GB; BMM fitting is 4.6 seconds of a 121-second ResNet-50 epoch
strongest_result: average gains of 1.4 points on synthetic benchmarks and 0.7 on real-noise benchmarks; ViT-B/16 CIFAR-100 instance-noise result is 92.24 percent
reported_limitations: two-stage history collection is still required; two augmented forwards per sample; label classification only; wrong-event mixture degrades under extreme noise because distributions become imbalanced
direct_prior_risk: critical: direct prior for low-cost joint cleanliness difficulty scoring and dynamic weighting
audit_notes: Deep-read 2026-07-31. This is the main killer of proposals based only on low-cost temporal statistics or hard-clean preservation. A new mechanism needs information or an objective not expressible by wrong-event BMM weighting.

title: Enhancing Sample Selection Against Label Noise by Cutting Mislabeled Easy Examples
clean_reference_required: no clean reference; 10 percent noisy training data is used for validation and threshold choices
extra_models: iterative models; appendix training uses two networks with cross-predictions
core_mechanism: starts from early-learned samples; at a later stopping state removes candidates with top loss top confidence and low input-gradient norm; repeats selection and retraining; per-round retention is set so total retention equals one minus the noise rate
main_claim: mislabeled-easy examples learned early can be more damaging than later-learned noise and should be cut using later-state recalibration
mechanism_evidence: CIFAR-10/100 CIFAR-N WebVision and full ImageNet-1K; influence-function support for the MEE observation; threshold and component ablations
efficiency_reported: three refinement rounds plus final training up to 300 epochs; on one RTX 4090 original CIFAR-100 ResNet-34 takes about 15.3 hours and faster one-round variant about nine hours; the MEE filter itself is under one percent but base iterative retraining dominates
strongest_result: CIFAR-100N Fine reaches 66.52 percent and full ImageNet-1K with 40-percent symmetric noise reaches 73.28 percent; faster variant loses only 0.41 point on CIFAR-100 symmetric 40 percent
reported_limitations: requires a noise-rate estimate to set retained fraction; visual classification only; theory is observational; iterative retraining is expensive; severe imbalance can confuse minority hard-clean examples with MEEs
direct_prior_risk: critical: direct prior for identifying harmful mislabeled-easy samples separately from hard-clean samples
audit_notes: Deep-read 2026-07-31. The paper's claim that Early Cutting overhead is below one percent refers only to its added filter, not the full iterative framework. Total training is 9-15 hours on RTX 4090.

title: Debiased Sample Selection for Learning with Noisy Labels
extra_models: one network for DSS; two networks for DSS+
core_mechanism: MDA divides predictions by an EMA class marginal to counter easy-class over-selection; CCS applies a Mann-Kendall trend test to candidate classes and excludes likely-true alternatives from the denominator so wrong annotations cannot suppress them
main_claim: class-level and instance-level confirmation bias can be removed with lightweight plug-ins while preserving hard samples and avoiding unsafe relabeling
mechanism_evidence: CIFAR-10/100 with four noise types; CIFAR-N Clothing1M WebVision and ILSVRC12; selector precision recall and trajectory case studies; CLIP compatibility
efficiency_reported: DSS trains 150 epochs; authors describe MDA and CCS as lightweight but do not report end-to-end wall-clock VRAM or trajectory-storage overhead in the main paper; DSS+ adds a second network and consistency regularization
strongest_result: DSS improves CIFAR-10 instance-dependent 50-percent noise by about 10 points over its BASE; DSS+ reports 94.74 on CIFAR-10N-Worst 74.67 on CIFAR-100N-Noisy and 82.40 on WebVision
reported_limitations: no dedicated limitations section; classification-label noise only; uniform target marginal needs modification for true long tails; trajectory storage and Mann-Kendall scaling are not costed; DSS+ is not a single-model method
direct_prior_risk: critical: direct prior for hard-sample preservation class calibration and trajectory-based bias correction
audit_notes: Deep-read 2026-07-31. Any proposal using confidence trends, class-marginal correction, candidate-label masking, or generic hard-clean rescue is directly anticipated.

title: What is Your Data Worth to GPT? LLM-Scale Data Valuation with Influence Functions
peft_method: LOGRA projection resembles LoRA but is an attribution tool
clean_reference_required: query or test gradients are required
extra_training_stages: post-hoc gradient logging then repeated queries
core_mechanism: exploits Kronecker structure to project per-example gradients from O(nk) to O(sqrt(nk)); stores projected training gradients once and answers influence queries by low-dimensional inverse-Hessian and vector similarity operations
main_claim: influence-function valuation can scale to billion-parameter models and billion-token data if gradient projection compute and memory are controlled
mechanism_evidence: counterfactual removal tests plus 1B-token OpenWebText attribution on 1.4B-8B models; qualitative query-attribution examples
efficiency_reported: all-example gradients still cost about one training epoch; Llama-3-8B LOGRA logging uses 23GB at batch one and 79GB at batch 16; projected gradients occupy 3.5TB; influence throughput is up to 6500 times EKFAC and memory 14-15GB versus 75GB
strongest_result: competitive counterfactual valuation accuracy and 79003.9 train-test pairs per second for large batches on one A100 80GB
reported_limitations: susceptible to large-gradient outliers; storage rather than compute limits the demonstrated corpus; attribution is post-hoc and query-dependent rather than online allocation; raw one-epoch logging is still unaffordable in the target regime
direct_prior_risk: critical: kills novelty of generic efficient gradient-based sample valuation
audit_notes: Deep-read 2026-07-31. LOGRA does not itself train a noise-robust model. It is nevertheless the required high-end valuation baseline and shows why a 5080 method must avoid per-example full-model gradients and terabyte-scale logs.

title: Distributional Training Data Attribution: What do Influence Functions Sample?
clean_reference_required: yes for the pruning objective: validation loss defines which points to remove
extra_models: multiple independently trained models represent the training distribution
core_mechanism: treats initialization and batching as a distribution over trained models; defines mean variance and Wasserstein influence; proves influence functions arise as a limiting distributional response; ranks removals by influence averaged over seeds
main_claim: single-run deterministic attribution misses distributional effects of unavoidable training randomness
mechanism_evidence: theory; 50-run small-model studies; ten-seed SWIN CIFAR-10 pruning; five-seed ArtBench diffusion attribution; distributional LDS with 20 subsets and 50 seeds
efficiency_reported: SWIN pruning trains ten full models then ten retrained models after removing 5000 points; distributional LDS trains 50 models for each of 20 subdatasets; hardware and total wall-clock are not disclosed despite checklist language
strongest_result: averaging influence over ten SWIN seeds yields better CIFAR-10 pruning than seed-specific subsets; Wasserstein influence exposes variance changes invisible to mean influence
reported_limitations: not a noisy-data training method; compute is fundamentally incompatible with a strict single-GPU budget; signal-to-noise for leave-one-out shifts can require many empirical samples; theoretical results rely on long-time and regularity assumptions
direct_prior_risk: critical evaluation prior: sample value claims must address training randomness
audit_notes: Deep-read 2026-07-31. The paper does not require every practical method to run many seeds online, but it forbids calling one deterministic trajectory an expected marginal value without a stability or distributional validation argument.
